newsitem.title: PARAGUAY: Paraguay ex-president acted in name of democracy.
newsitem.headline: Paraguay ex-president acted in name of democracy.

text.p: Paraguay's Gen. Andres Rodriguez, who died in New York on Monday, toppled dictator Alfredo Stroessner in 1989 "in the name of democracy" but was widely suspected of using his power to line his pockets with drug money.
Rodriguez's presidency paved the way for democratic elections in 1993 won by Juan Carlos Wasmosy but was plagued with charges of drug-related corruption and nepotism.

A short, stocky cavalry officer, Rodriguez was known before the coup as an unswerving supporter of General Stroessner, who ruled for nearly 35 years, longer than any other ruler in the Western Hemisphere, before his ouster.

Rodriguez underwent surgery for colorectal cancer at the Sloan-Kettering Memorial Hospital in New York on Jan. 23 and returned a month later for further surgery after the cancer spread to his liver, a hospital spokeswoman said. He developed complications including kidney failure during the last week and died on Monday morning. He was 73.

Born in June 1923 of farming stock, Rodriguez graduated from Military College in 1946. He was appointed provisional commander of the First Cavalry Division in 1961, major-general in 1970 and commander of the First Army Corps in 1982.
He became one of the richest men in Paraguay as Stroessner's protege and his home in Asuncion is a replica of France's Fontainebleau chateau.

Rodriguez's estrangement from Stroessner may have been linked to the government's closure of foreign exchange houses in late January 1989 to stop speculation. Rodriguez owned the country's biggest exchange house, Cambio Guarani, as well as a fleet of trucks, an air cargo company, a brewery and vast farms with tens of thousands of head of cattle.

Rumours that Latin America's longest-ruling dictator was about to force Rodriguez to retire appear to have sparked the bloody two-day coup in which up to 300 people are thought to have died, although the official death toll was 17.

Rodriguez quickly called the first free elections in the country's history in May 1989, purged the armed forces of Stroessner men and legalised all political parties except the Communists. He went on to win the elections amid widespread allegations of vote-rigging.

In 1992 his opponents forced a constitutional amendment forbidding Rodriguez or any blood relative from standing for president in the future. In exchange, he became a lifetime senator, giving him immunity from prosecution on charges of drug trafficking swirling around him since the 1970s.

In 1993 he was accused of using anti-drugs operations as a cover for his own cocaine-smuggling business but judges refused to admit any evidence and the case was dropped. In 1996 he was again accused and named in investigations into the murder of a drug squad chief two years earlier, but his immunity as a senator saved him once again.

Rodriguez's most unquestionable achievement for his country, besides putting an end to Stroessner's iron rule, was his role in the 1991 Treaty of Asuncion, which founded the Mercosur regional trade bloc with Paraguay's giant neighbours Brazil and Argentina, with Uruguay as a fourth partner.
